proposals.compressedText:
# Field Guide: Preparing a Home for a 72-Hour Power Outage

Prepare an ordinary household to stay safe and comfortable through a power outage of up to seventy-two hours. Assumes a temperate climate and no backup generator. Work the sections in order; the earlier ones matter most.

## Water

Store four litres per person per day, so twelve litres per person for the full seventy-two hours: half for drinking, half for cooking and basic hygiene. Use food-grade containers, keep them out of direct sunlight, and replace stored water every six months. With advance warning of a storm, also fill the bathtub; use bathtub water for flushing toilets and washing, never for drinking.

## Food

Keep a dedicated shelf of non-perishable food for three days: canned beans, canned fish, peanut butter, crackers, dried fruit, and shelf-stable milk. Choose foods needing no cooking, and own a manual can opener, since an electric one is useless. Eat the refrigerator's perishable food first, then the freezer's, and only then the emergency shelf.

## Refrigerator and freezer

An unopened refrigerator keeps food safe about four hours. A full freezer holds a safe temperature about forty-eight hours, a half-full one only about twenty-four, so keep it consolidated and full, even with containers of frozen water. Keep both doors closed as much as possible and tape a reminder note to each. Discard any perishable food more than two hours above four degrees Celsius; when in doubt, throw it out.

## Light

Use battery-powered LED lanterns or headlamps as your primary light, and avoid candles entirely, a leading cause of house fires during outages. Store at least one light per person plus two spare sets of batteries for each. Keep one headlamp beside each bed and one lantern in the kitchen, placed where they can be found in the dark.

## Heat and safety

Never run a camping stove, barbecue, or generator indoors, in a garage, or near a window; each produces carbon monoxide, which is odourless and can be fatal. Install at least one battery-powered carbon monoxide alarm on each floor where people sleep. In cold weather, pick one small room on a south-facing side, close its door, and gather everyone; layered clothing and blankets beat any improvised heater. If the indoor temperature falls below ten degrees Celsius and you cannot stay warm, relocate to a warming centre or a neighbour's home.

## Communication and information

Keep a battery-powered or hand-crank radio for emergency broadcasts, and learn your local emergency station's frequency before the outage. Charge every phone and power bank whenever a storm is forecast; a full twenty-thousand-milliamp-hour power bank recharges a typical phone roughly four times. Put your phone in low-power mode as the outage starts, and agree in advance on one out-of-area contact everyone will text, because texts beat voice calls on congested networks.

## Medical needs

Keep a first-aid kit and a seven-day supply of every prescription medication, rotating them to stay in date. Refrigerated medication such as insulin generally stays usable at room temperature up to twenty-eight days, but confirm the rule for your medication with a pharmacist before an emergency. Write your pharmacy, doctor, and poison-control numbers on paper, because a dead phone is not a phone book.

## When the power returns

Wait five minutes before switching major appliances back on, letting the grid stabilise. Check the freezer: food still holding ice crystals can be safely refrozen. Restock everything used within one week, starting with water and batteries. Finally, write a one-page note on what was missing or awkward, and fix at least one gap before the next outage.

proposals.title: Restructure: collapse preamble, merge prose into dense fact-lists
proposals.rationale: Structure-level only: collapse the three-sentence preamble to two, and convert every section body from paragraphs into bullet lists that pack each fact onto one line (e.g. the three fridge/freezer holding times as one bullet, the water allowance and its split as one bullet). No fact, quantity, duration, temperature, item, or ordered step is removed; connective narration between them is what shrinks. Lists chosen over a table because the counting rule tokenises spaced pipes, so a table inflates the metric.
proposals.hardConstraintNote: Remains a self-contained instruction document: full title, all eight sections in the original order, every command/item/number/ordered step verbatim, plus the framing (up to seventy-two hours, temperate climate, no generator, work in order). A reader can act on it end to end with nothing external.

# Field Guide: Preparing a Home for a 72-Hour Power Outage

Prepare an ordinary household to manage safely and comfortably through a power outage lasting up to seventy-two hours. Assumes a temperate climate and no backup generator. Work the sections in order; the earlier ones matter most.

## Water
- Store four litres per person per day = twelve litres per person for the full seventy-two hours; half for drinking, half for cooking and basic hygiene.
- Use food-grade containers kept out of direct sunlight; replace stored water every six months.
- If a storm is forecast and you have advance warning, also fill the bathtub — that water is for flushing toilets and washing, never for drinking.

## Food
- Keep a dedicated shelf of non-perishable, no-cook food for three days: canned beans, canned fish, peanut butter, crackers, dried fruit, shelf-stable milk.
- Own a manual can opener, because an electric one will be useless.
- Eat in order: perishable food from the refrigerator first, then the freezer, and only then the emergency shelf.

## Refrigerator and freezer
- Safe holding times: an unopened refrigerator about four hours; a full freezer about forty-eight hours; a half-full freezer about twenty-four hours.
- Keep both doors closed as much as possible and tape a reminder note to each door.
- Keep the freezer consolidated and full, even if some space is containers of frozen water.
- Discard any perishable food that has spent more than two hours above four degrees Celsius; when in doubt, throw it out.

## Light
- Primary source: battery-powered LED lanterns or headlamps. Avoid candles entirely, since they are a leading cause of house fires during outages.
- Store at least one light per person plus two spare sets of batteries for each light.
- Keep one headlamp beside each bed and one lantern in the kitchen; place them where they can be found in the dark.

## Heat and safety
- Never run a camping stove, barbecue, or generator indoors, in a garage, or near a window: each produces carbon monoxide, which is odourless and can be fatal.
- Install at least one battery-powered carbon monoxide alarm on each floor where people sleep.
- In cold weather, choose one small room on a south-facing side of the home, close its door, and gather everyone there; layered clothing and blankets are safer than any improvised heater.
- If the indoor temperature falls below ten degrees Celsius and you cannot maintain warmth, relocate to a warming centre or a neighbour's home.

## Communication and information
- Keep a battery-powered or hand-crank radio for emergency broadcasts, and know your local emergency station's frequency before the outage begins.
- When a storm is forecast, charge every phone and power bank; a full modern power bank of twenty thousand milliamp-hours will recharge a typical phone roughly four times.
- At the start of the outage, put your phone in low-power mode.
- Agree in advance on one out-of-area contact whom every member of the household will text, because texts get through congested networks more reliably than voice calls.

## Medical needs
- Keep a first-aid kit and a seven-day supply of every prescription medication, and rotate them so they stay in date.
- Refrigerated medication such as insulin generally remains usable at room temperature for up to twenty-eight days, but confirm the rule for your specific medication with a pharmacist before an emergency.
- Write the phone numbers of your pharmacy, your doctor, and the poison-control line on paper, because a dead phone is not a phone book.

## When the power returns
- Wait five minutes before switching major appliances back on, so the grid can stabilise.
- Check the freezer: if food still contains ice crystals, it can be safely refrozen.
- Restock everything used during the outage within one week, starting with water and batteries.
- Write a one-page note about what was missing or awkward, and fix at least one of those gaps before the next outage arrives.
